claims: Medicine-ball power assessment depends on a standardized throw task, ball mass, execution, and outcome measure.

{{canonicalName}} must define stance and orientation, one- or two-hand release, ball start position, primary force direction, rotational intent, entry steps, target or free-flight lane, catch or retrieval rule, and finish.
Medicine-ball throws are commonly used as upper-body plyometric or ballistic power exercises, but training protocols and throw positions vary.

Classify {{canonicalName}} by forward versus rotational force direction, bilateral versus unilateral release, chest-level versus underhand start, static versus dynamic entry, and wall, partner, or open-lane outcome.
Standing and seated medicine-ball throws are measurably different tasks, so lower-body contribution and whole-body coordination cannot be inferred from an upper-body-only label.
Represent the feet, ankles, knees, hips, pelvis, trunk, scapulae, shoulders, elbows, wrists, and hands actually used by the selected standing, kneeling, seated, or supine version.
Rotational medicine-ball power can be assessed from release velocity or throw distance when the protocol is standardized.

Coach pressure from the floor through the hips and trunk into the ball, preserve the intended forward or transverse vector, release without a lumbar-dominant twist or backward lean, and finish in a controlled stance.
Throw technique and medicine-ball mass affect performance variability and therefore change the demands of the task.

Score technical complexity, absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, failure consequence, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty directly. Athlete experience is programming context and never an exercise-card skill level.
Medicine-ball power performance can decline after upper-body neuromuscular fatigue.

{{canonicalName}} must track ball mass and type, throws and catches per side, entry contacts, release velocity or distance when measured, target accuracy, local shoulder and trunk fatigue, technical speed loss, recovery between sets, and weekly high-intent throw volume.
Reliable comparison requires the same technique and ball mass.

Require an intact appropriately sized medicine ball, a clear wall or open throwing lane matched to rebound behavior, safe retrieval space, a defined target and stop command, stable footing, athlete separation, and no bystanders in the flight or rebound path.
Upper-body plyometric studies use varied doses, with lower repetition ranges generally paired with maximal effort and adequate inter-set and inter-session recovery.

For power delivery, use roughly three to five sets of two to six high-quality throws per side or bilateral set with 60–180 seconds between sets; stop before speed, distance, accuracy, posture, or safe rebound control declines.
Measurement is meaningful only when the throwing protocol stays consistent.
State the stance, ball position, hand pattern, target, permitted step or rotation, release vector, catch or retrieval action, reset, side order, and exact rep-quality rule before the first throw.
Youth resistance and power training should be supervised, technically appropriate, progressively dosed, and performed with safe equipment and space.

Stop for pain, numbness, dizziness, unsafe ball rebound, target or wall failure, lane entry, loss of grip, uncontrolled catch, lumbar-dominant rotation, shoulder or elbow compensation, loss of balance, accuracy collapse, or repeatable output loss.
Upper-body plyometric training can improve medicine-ball throwing and sport-specific throwing performance, although certainty and transfer vary by task and population.
Place {{canonicalName}} early in Output work after relevant access and activation. Match stance, vector, ball mass, and intent to the objective; do not turn maximal throws into dense conditioning.
A medicine-ball throw can be repeatable when position, ball mass, trials, and measurement are standardized.

Show the exact front, side, and target views; label ball mass and rebound type; demonstrate start, load, release, follow-through, retrieval or catch, reset, side change, acceptable miss, and stop signal.
Velocity and distance can serve as field measures when the rotational medicine-ball protocol is controlled.

Provide ball-mass selection, lane and wall inspection, side balance, release-vector observation, target zones, optional velocity or distance tracking, speed-loss rules, catch counts, camera angles, regression decisions, and weekly throw-budget guidance.
Seated medicine-ball throwing can provide a reliable upper-body power task when lower-body contribution is intentionally constrained.

Accessibility options include a lighter or larger soft ball, seated or tall-kneeling support, shorter target distance, partner return instead of wall rebound, no catch, reduced rotation, pre-positioned ball, fewer throws, longer recovery, verbal and visual cues, and non-maximal familiarization.
Standing versus seated position, ball mass, and throw technique materially change the measured task.

Treat stance and entry as controlled variants when release pattern and vector stay the same; create a distinct definition when bilateral versus unilateral release, forward versus rotational vector, chest versus scoop path, overhead direction, rebound catch, or terminal outcome changes.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

Visible links for {{canonicalName}} remain candidate-only. Availability, embedding, exact stance and release match, full viewing, ball type, target and rebound behavior, captions, cue and safety quality, reviewer identity, and approval are separate gates.

assessmentSummary.identity: A static standing bilateral chest-level medicine-ball pass projected forward to a wall or partner, followed by a controlled catch or retrieval and full reset.
currentCardFindings: The current card describes horizontal upper-body power but does not define stance, hand position, permitted countermovement, target, rebound, catch, distance, ball mass, or reset.
The consolidated baseline variants repeat the same identity with conflicting Output and Capacity doses rather than controlled delivery profiles.

Uniform legacy difficulty values understate ball-rebound supervision, catch exposure, load-dependent release changes, and the distinction between standing, seated, kneeling, stepping, and reactive versions.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: release speed and target stay stable without backward lean, rib flare, unsafe rebound, or catch error

coachCues: Own the rebound or let it drop
athleteInstructions: Face the target, hold the ball at your chest, brace, drive both hands forward fast, then catch only if assigned and reset before the next rep

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain one standing bilateral forward chest-pass definition. Merge duplicate baseline variants after human review; express seated, kneeling, stepping, partner, wall, catch, and load choices as controlled variants or delivery annotations.

assessmentSummary.identity: A static side-on bilateral medicine-ball throw that loads the ball near the back hip and uses sequenced hip and trunk rotation to release low and laterally into a wall or open lane.
currentCardFindings: The current description identifies a side-on back-hip load but does not lock stance width, permitted pivot, release height, wall angle, target, catch rule, side balance, ball mass, or dynamic entry.
The kicking-specific consolidated source is a programming context, not a new exercise identity.
Legacy media includes forward-facing and facing-the-wall variants that may change the loading angle and must not silently define the static side-on baseline.

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as the static side-on bilateral rotational scoop definition. Treat sport transfer as profile metadata; step-behind, drop-step, shuffle, through-swing, kneeling, and facing-wall entries are controlled variants.
